metadata.title: Characterization of Antimicrobial Peptide Produced by Bacillus Subtilis Subsp. Subtilis
metadata.description:
Abstract Purpose: Antimicrobial peptides are amongst the most promising class of peptides to contract the rise of global antimicrobial resistant. This article investigates a new antimicrobial peptide from bacteria.Methods: Bacterial identification was based on phenotypical and biochemical properties as well as 16S rRNA gene sequence homology. Bacterial growth and production of the inhibitory substance was standardized and optimized. The newly antimicrobial peptide was purified to homogeneity, subsequently analyzed by PAGE and MALDI-TOF-MS.Results: The bacterium identified as Bacillus subtilis subsp. subtilis and designated as strain MZ-32. Landy medium was best for the production when compared with different media after fixing the least influential variables in standardized fermentation conditions. Carbohydrate and nitrogen supplements investigated to improve production in Landy medium. The antimicrobial peptide of 2.158-Da was active against a broad range of skin-born pathogenic bacteria that were resistant to standard antibiotics, and possessed the physico-chemical properties of an ideal antimicrobial agent in terms of water solubility, thermal resistance, and stability towards acid/alkali (pH 4.0 to 9.0) treatments.Conclusion: The new strain and its associated peptide are potentially new candidates for medical and biotechnological applications.

metadata.title: A Cyclic Antimicrobial Peptide Produced in Primate Leukocytes by the Ligation of Two Truncated -Defensins
metadata.description: Analysis of rhesus macaque leukocytes disclosed the presence of an 18-residue macrocyclic, tridisulfide antibiotic peptide in granules of neutrophils and monocytes. The peptide, termed rhesus theta defensin-1 (RTD-1), is microbicidal for bacteria and fungi at low micromolar concentrations. Antibacterial activity of the cyclic peptide was threefold greater than that of an open-chain analog, and the cyclic conformation was required for antimicrobial activity in the presence of 150 millimolar sodium chloride. Biosynthesis of RTD-1 involves the head-to-tail ligation of two α-defensin–related nonapeptides, requiring the formation of two new peptide bonds. Thus, host defense cells possess mechanisms for synthesis and granular packaging of macrocyclic antibiotic peptides that are components of the phagocyte antimicrobial armamentarium.

metadata.title: PeptiDesCalculator: Software for computation of peptide descriptors. Definition, implementation and case studies for 9 bioactivity endpoints
metadata.description: We present a novel Java-based program denominated PeptiDesCalculator for computing peptide descriptors. These descriptors include: redefinitions of known protein parameters to suite the peptide domain, generalization schemes for the global descriptions of peptide characteristics, as well as empirical descriptors based on experimental evidence on peptide stability and interaction propensity. The PeptiDesCalculator software provides a user-friendly Graphical User Interface (GUI) and is parallelized to maximize the use of computational resources available in current work stations. The PeptiDesCalculator indices are employed in modeling 8 peptide bioactivity endpoints demonstrating satisfactory behavior. Moreover, we compare the performance of a support vector machine (SVM) classifier built using 15 PeptiDesCalculator indices with that of a recently reported deep neural network (DNN) antimicrobial activity classifier, demonstrating comparable test set performance notwithstanding the remarkably lower degree of freedom for the former. This software will facilitate the development of in silico models for the prediction of peptide properties.

metadata.title: Self-Assembly of Branching and Linear Synthetic Polycationic Peptides in Phosphate Buffer and Its Impact on Antimicrobial Activity
metadata.description: Among therapeutic peptides, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) have gained significant attention for their potential to combat antimicrobial resistance. Their efficacy often relies on the ability to adopt organized structures, such as alpha-helices or beta-strands. However, the formation of supramolecular aggregates can hinder their antimicrobial effectiveness. This study explores the correlation between supramolecular organization in phosphate buffer (PB) and biological activity in three cationic peptides with identical amino acid compositions, nine Leu-Lys pairs, but differing architectures: linear and branched, using lysine or a triazine as the branching unit. Structural conformation and self-assembly behaviors in water and PB were analyzed using Circular Dichroism (CD), Dynamic Light Scattering, and Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM). Results show that the linear peptide, largely unstructured or randomly coiled in water at neutral pH, adopts a beta-sheet conformation in PB. AFM imaging revealed that at low peptide and phosphate concentrations, the linear peptide showed small helical rods self-assembled via beta-sheet interactions. This structural transition is driven by electrostatic interactions between phosphate ions and the amine group. The linear peptide, which lacks antibacterial activity, shows a strong tendency to form large beta-strand aggregates. In contrast, branched peptides were less prone to aggregation and showed enhanced antibacterial activity, particularly the triazine-branched peptide.

metadata.title: Multifunctional Acidocin 4356 combats Pseudomonas aeruginosa through membrane perturbation and virulence attenuation: Experimental results confirmed molecular dynamic simulation
metadata.description:
A longstanding awareness in generating resistance to common antimicrobial therapies by gram-negative bacteria has made them a major threat to global health. The application of antimicrobial peptides as a therapeutic agent would be a great opportunity to combat bacterial diseases. Here, we introduce a new antimicrobial peptide (∼8.5 kDa) from probiotic strain Lactobacillus acidophilus ATCC 4356, designated as Acidocin 4356 (ACD). This multifunctional peptide exerts its anti-infective ability against Pseudomonas aeruginosa through an inhibitory action on virulence factors, bacterial killing, and biofilm degradation. Reliable performance over tough physiological conditions and low hemolytic activity confirmed a new hope for the therapeutic setting. Antibacterial kinetic studies using flow cytometry technique showed that the ACD activity is related to the change in permeability of the membrane. The results obtained from molecular dynamic (MD) simulation were perfectly suited to the experimental data of ACD behavior. The structure-function relationship of this natural compound, along with the results of TEM analysis and molecular dynamic (MD) simulation, confirmed the ability of the ACD aimed at enhancing bacterial membrane perturbation. The peptide was effective in the treatment of P. aeruginosa infection in mouse model. The results support the therapeutic potential of ACD for the treatment of Pseudomonas infections.

Importance Multidrug-resistant bacteria are a major threat to global health, and Pseudomonas bacterium with the ability to form biofilms has considered as one of the main causative agents of nosocomial infections. Traditional antibiotics have failed because of increased resistance. So, finding new biocompatible antibacterial drugs are essential. Antimicrobial peptides are produced by various organisms as a natural defense mechanism against pathogens, inspiring for the possible design of the next generation of antibiotics. In this study, a new antimicrobial peptide was isolated from Lactobacillus acidophilus ATCC 4356, counteracting both biofilm and planktonic cells of P. aeruginosa. A detailed investigation was then conducted concerning the functional mechanism of this peptide by using fluorescence techniques, electron microscopy, and in silico methods. The antibacterial and antibiofilm properties of this peptide may be important in the treatment of Pseudomonas infections.

metadata.title: Overcoming Drug Resistance: The Promise of Peptide-Based Antimicrobials
metadata.description:
Abstract....

Antimicrobial treatments using antimicrobial peptides are increasing day by day due to significant rise in the drug resistance infections. They play important role in the innate immune system in many organisms like humans. They are also very effective against the many pathogens such as parasites, some fungi, many viruses, and bacteria. Antimicrobial peptides are usually investigated as therapies to address the problems causing by antibiotic resistance. It is because; they have strong antibacterial qualities but fewer tendencies to cause resistance. Antimicrobial are classified into many types and each type have significant applications. They act as front line defenders for the treatment of infectious diseases. Their complexities involved their large scaled production.

Introduction

Antimicrobial resistance is the global health issue nowadays that requires the new therapeutic processes. In the solutions regarding these issues, antimicrobial peptides play important role and got attention because of their wide range of antimicrobial activities and low tendency for creating the resistances. They target specific bacterial enzyme and pathways in organisms. They breakdown the microbial membranes and make them harder for pathogens to develop more resistance(Haney et al., 2017).

Antimicrobial peptides are the short peptides, usually range from 10-5 amino acids in their length. They consist of very complex structures having alpha helix, beta sheets, coiled structures and ringed looped conformations. Their structural diversity reinforces their interactions with the membranes of microbes and their functional adaptability. They have amphipathic nature i.e., hydrophobic and hydrophilic regions that enables them to select specific interactions with the microbial membranes and cause less damage to host cells.  This feature makes them a diverse tool in combating infections(Sierra et al., 2017).

In spite of their antimicrobial properties, they are also used for their immunomodulatory functions. They improve the immune response of host by increasing immune cells at the infection sites and increase phagocytosis, and enhance cytokine production. These roles make it multi-functional agents and have vast variety of applications. We will have a detailed look into AMPs, their structure and mechanism of action to applications in clinical development(Cederlund et al., 2011).

History and sources of antimicrobial peptides

Antimicrobial peptides are known as oligo-peptides ranging from 5-100 amino acids. They have broad range of targeted organisms from viruses to parasites. Historically, antimicrobial peptides act as cationic and anionic host defense peptides, cationic amphipathic peptides, only cationic antimicrobial peptides, host defense peptides and alpha helical AMPs(Lazzaro et al., 2020).

In 1939, antimicrobial peptides are discovered by Dubos, when he extracted an agent from the stain of soil Bacillus. He used this strain for the mice to protect it from pneumococci infection. Also in this year, Hotchkiss and Dubos make fractions of this extract (fractionation) and identified a new antimicrobial peptide and named it as gramicidin. Gramicidin found very effective for the treatment of ulcers and wounds but it cause toxicity in the intra-peritoneal applications. One more antimicrobial peptide discovered named as tyrocidine and it found to be very good against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. But it showed toxicity against human blood cells. In this year, one more effective antimicrobial peptide against fungi and some pathogenic bacteria were found named as purothionin(George et al., 2023).

In 1956, the first AMP originated from animal is defensin, it was extracted from the leukocytes of Rabbit. Two more AMPs are discovered, one from epithelia named as bombinin and other from cow milk named as lactoferrin. At this time, it was proved that AMPs present in human leukocytes are located in their lysosomes(Pelaez, 2006).

Now, more than 5000 AMPs have been discovered. In prokaryotes such as bacteria and eukaryotes such as protozoan, fungi, plants, insects and animals, natural AMPs are present. In animals, antimicrobial peptides are mostly present in tissues and organs that are more visible to airborne microbes. They act as the first line defense of innate immune system against the many pathogens like bacteria, fungi, and viruses. In this way, AMPs play a role in preventing infections before entering into body or showing any symptoms. For example, skin of frog act as the source of more than 300 AMPs(Dini et al., 2022).

Many types of eukaryotic cells also produced antimicrobial peptides such as in gastrointestinal and genitourinary system; epithelial cells produced AMPs, lymph and lymphocytes of the immune system. Antimicrobial peptides are involved in innate immunity, producing inflammatory responses during any infection. Bacteria produced lipopolysaccharides molecules resulting from antibiotic treatment or according to host’s immunity and these lipopolysaccharides induces AMPs in mammals.

Structure and Major Activities of AMPs

Based on their secondary structures, the majority of AMPs that have been described so far can be divided into four categories: loop, beta-sheet, alpha-helix and extended. Alpha helical peptides are the most researched AMPs to date, and alpha helix and beta sheet structures are more widespread among these structural categories. Two adjacent amino acids in alpha helix structures are separated by about 0.15nm and have an angle of around 100 degrees with respect to the center(Ahmed & Hammami, 2019). Among these AMPs, protegrin, magainin, cyclic indolicin, and coiled indolicin are the most well-known. A minimum of two beta strands with disulfide bonds connecting them make up beta sheets peptides.

Although the majority of AMPs fall into one of the four classifications, certain AMPs are not included in any of these categories. Two distant structural elements are present in certain AMPs. Also, a lot of peptides only build their active structure when they intact with target cell membranes. For example, in aqueous solutions, indolicin exhibits globular and amphipathic conformation, present in surroundings that mimic lipid bilayers in wedge shape. Moreover, antimicrobial peptides also change its conformation when it interacts with DNA, by a slight shift in the wavelength of extreme emission and a drop in fluorescence intensity(Zhang et al., 2021). AMPs target the lipopolysaccharide layer of the cell membrane, which is present in all microbes, in contrast to probable antibiotics, which target certain biological functions (such as the creation of DNA, proteins, or cell walls). Eukaryotic cells are outside of many AMPs target range due to their high cholesterol content and low anionic charge. The quick lethal impact of AMPs is another significant characteristic. Certain AMPs have the ability to kill within seconds of first coming into contact with the cell membrane. It is also known that AMPs have synergistic effects that increase the activity of antibiotics(Bulet et al., 1999).

Since amino acids are used to make AMPs, changing their structure including library construction and screening and immobilizing them on surfaces is very simple. Fully synthetic peptides can be produced by recombinant expression methods or chemical synthesis. These synthetic AMP sources can be used to create new synthetic AMPs and modify already existing AMPs. Modifications of this kind may change the targets of AMPs and increase their resistance to proteases. Notwithstanding these positive characteristics, AMPs still face certain obstacles in their use, including the possibility of human toxicity, sensitivity to harsh environmental factors (such as high pH and protease susceptibility), lack of selectively against specific strains, high production costs, problems with folding of some large AMPs, decreased activity when applied to surfaces, and bacterial resistance to some AMPs(Li et al., 2021).

Major categories of AMPs

Classification

In general, AMPs antibacterial properties do not break enzymatic processes. For example, as lysozyme is a monomeric peptide, it is not defined as an AMP due to its relatively large size and ability to kill bacteria by breaking 1, 4-K-links in peptidoglycan chains through enzymatic activity.

1. Antiviral peptides

By integrating into the host cell membrane or the viral envelope, antiviral AMPs kill viruses. Viral envelopes may become fragile due to AMP integration, which inhibits the viruses from infecting host cells. Additionally, AMPs can lower the virus’s ability to connect to host cells. Defensins, for example, attach to the viral glycoproteins, which prevents herpes simplex viruses (HSV) from attaching to the host cell surface(Agarwal & Gabrani, 2021).

Some specific antiviral AMPs can stop viral particles from entering host cells by engaging specific receptors on mammalian cells; also it disrupts viral envelopes and inhibiting viral receptors. Heparan sulfate, for example, is important for the HSV viral particles to adhere to the surface of the host cells. Glycosaminoglycan molecules with a negative charge make up heparin sulfate(Vilas Boas et al., 2019). Therefore, by binding to heparan molecules and preventing virus-receptor interactions, specifically alpha-helical cationic peptides, such as lactoferrin, can stop HSV infections. Some Specific AMPs are not able to compete with viral glycoproteins for binding to the cell surface heparan sulfate receptors. Antiviral AMPs have the ability to penetrate the cell membrane and settle in the cytoplasm and organelles, changing the host cells gene expression profile. This can either protect the production of viral genes or helps the host defense system in eliminating viruses(Chang & Yang, 2013).

2. Antibacterial peptides

Antibacterial AMPs are cationic AMPs that target bacterial cell membranes and cause the lipid bilayer structure to collapse, establishing them the most researched AMPs to date. They have both hydrophilic and hydrophobic domains, creating them amphipathic in nature. These structural abilities make them able to attach to phospholipid groups as hydrophilic region and lipid components as hydrophobic region(Otvos, 2000).

Some AMPs can kill bacteria at low concentrations without maintaining the integrity of their membranes. These AMPs kill bacteria by inhibiting essential internal procedures like DNA replication and protein synthesis, by directly interacting with the membrane. For example, Buforin II may penetrate inside cells and bind itself to RNA and DNA without causing harm to the cell membrane. Apidaecin, pyrrhocoricin, and drososin are other example of it. These AMPs consist of an active site for their intracellular target and 18-20 amino acid residues.

In some cases, AMPs can eliminate germs that are resistance to antibiotics.  For example, the formation of cell walls can be blocked by both the antibiotic vancomycin and the AMP nisin. Nevertheless, it has been reported that a strain of methicillin-resistance Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is resistance to vancomycin but remains vulnerable to nisin(Boman, 2003).

3. Antifungal peptides

Antifungal peptides, like antibacterial AMPs, can abolish fungus by going after their internal components or cell wall. That’s why, the components of a fungal cell wall and a bacterial membrane differs. For example, many antifungal peptides have the ability to combine with the chitin, which are main elements of fungal cell walls(Fernández de Ullivarri et al., 2020). These capabilities of binding, helps AMPs to effectively target fungal cell. Cell wall targets the antifungal AMPs that disrupt the target cells either by directly forming pores or by enhancing the permeabilization of plasma membrane or sometime rupturing the membrane’s integrity. Most of the antifungal AMPs have neutral and polar amino acids in their structures, so they does not seem to be a correlation between the cells type that it should targets and the antifungal AMPs structure(Rautenbach et al., 2016).

4. Antiparasitic peptides

If we compare to other three peptides, Antiparasitic ones are a smaller group. The first known Antiparasitic peptide was magainin, which has ability to eradicate Paramecium Caudatum. After sometime, a new synthetic peptide was created that combats the Leishmania parasite. Another example of Antiparasitic peptide was developed having ability to kill Caernohabditis elegans by creating holes in its cells membrane, known as cathelicidin. Also, these AMPs work in the same manner as others, despite the fact that some parasitic microorganisms are multicellular and they communicate directly with the cell membrane to cause cell death(Pretzel et al., 2013).

 

Figure 1: Classification of AMPs

Some Properties of AMPs:

1. Length

As, amphipathic structural properties with hydrophobic and hydrophilic faces on opposite sides of a peptide molecule need at least 7-8 amino acids, an AMP’s length affects its activity. In the barrel-stave model, an AMP should have at least 22 amino acids to cross the lipid bilayer of bacteria, whereas beta sheet AMPs requires 8 amino acids. An AMP’s length should have an impact on its cytotoxicity to its 3D structure. For example, a shorter derivative of HP(2-20) and a shortened melittin with 15 amino acid residues at the C-terminal revealed minimum 300 times less toxicity to erythrocytes of human and rat, in comparison with their original forms. So that, when creating novel synthetic peptides that have low toxicity, the length of antimicrobial peptide should be taken into care(Gagnon et al., 2017).

2. Net charge

The initial cause of the first interaction with negatively charged cell membranes is the net charge of known AMPs, which is the total of all charges of the peptide’s ionizable groups and ranges from negative to positive. AMPs hemolytic and antibacterial properties can be altered by adjusting its net charge that will be able to kill microorganisms selectively while having a bit no impact on host cells. For example, raising V13K’s positive net charge from +8 to +9 levels up its hemolytic activity, whereas decreasing the net charge to less than +4 demolished its property to disrupt P. aeruginosa(Jindal et al., 2014).

3.  Helicity

The ability of an AMP to create spin structure is called as Helicity. In contrast to other elements of AMPs, Helicity is the less specific. Nonetheless, it is critical for finding out how harmful it is to eukaryotic cells. It has been figured that lowering Helicity by addition of D- amino acids to the primary sequence decreases the hemolytic effect while maintaining antibacterial activity.

For instance, some alpha helical peptides are found to lose their hemolytic activity when 35% of the L-amino acids were exchanged with D-amino acids. Moreover, these synthetic AMPs are protease insensitive. In order to develop new synthetic peptides with decreased hemolytic activity and enhanced stability against proteolytic cleavage, it is very helpful to integrate D-amino acids to alter Helicity(Huang et al., 2014).

The helix propensity of all amino acids in the main sequence is a crucial factor linked to the Helicity of AMP. Proline and glycine, for instance, are less likely than other amino acids to form helices. So that, when they are developing alpha helical AMPs, these residues are not recommended. Additionally, peptides should possess sufficient flexibility to change their structure throughput the membrane insertion procedure(Chen et al., 2007).

metadata.title: Identification and characterization of three novel antimicrobial peptides from the marine mollusk Nerita versicolor (Gmelin, 1791).
metadata.description: Mollusks have been widely investigated for antimicrobial peptides, because their humoral defense against pathogens is mainly based on such small biomolecules. In this report, we describe the identification of three novel antimicrobial peptides from the marine mollusk Nerita versicolor. A pool of N. versicolor peptides was analyzed by nanoLC-ESI-MS-MS technology and three potential antimicrobial peptides (Nv-p1, Nv-p2 and Nv-p3) were identified by bioinformatical predictions and selected for chemical synthesis and evaluation of their biological activity. Database searches showed that two of them shows partial identity to Histone H4 peptide fragments from other invertebrate species. Structural predictions revealed that they all adopt a random coil structure even when placed near a lipid bilayer patch. Nv-p1, Nv-p2 and Nv-p3 exhibited activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The most active peptide was Nv-p3 with an inhibitory activity of starting at 1.5 µg/mL in radial diffusion assays. The peptides were ineffective against Klebsiella pneumoniae, Listeria monocytogenes, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. On the other hand, these peptides demonstrated effective antibiofilm action against Candida albicans, Candida parapsilosis and Candida auris, but not against the planktonic cells. None of the peptides had significant toxicity on primary human macrophages and fetal lung fibroblasts at effective antimicrobial concentrations. Our results indicate that N. versicolor-derived peptides represent new AMP sequences and have the potential to be optimized and developed into antibiotic alternatives against bacterial and fungal infections.

metadata.title: The design and functional characterization of a novel hybrid antimicrobial peptide from Esculentin-1a and melittin
metadata.description: Antimicrobial agents are one of the most widely used drugs in medicine. In the last fifty years, the misuse of these agents caused the emergence of resistant strains of bacteria that led to an increase in life-threatening infections. The need to develop new agents has become a priority, and antimicrobial peptides attained high consideration. The antimicrobial activities of a novel In-house designed hybrid cationic peptide (BKR1) were studied against different strains of Gram-negative bacteria. This was done using the broth dilution method as outlined by the Clinical and Laboratory Institute (CLSI). Checkerboard assy was employed to investigate the synergistic activity of BKR1 peptide with four antibiotics (Levofloxacin, chloramphenicol, rifampicin, and ampicillin). Finally, the cytotoxicity of BKR1 was evaluated against human blood cells and mammalian kidney cells (Vero cells). BKR1 displayed bactericidal activity against tested strains of Gram-negative bacteria, with zero hemolytic effects. It also acts as a strong adjuvant with levofloxacin, chloramphenicol, and rifampicin against resistant strains of P. aeruginosa and E. coli. This study represents the design and elucidation of the antimicrobial activities of a novel hybrid antimicrobial peptide named (BKR1). Our results indicate thar BKR1 is a promising candidate to treat resistant infectious diseases individually or as an adjuvant with conventional antibiotics.

metadata.title: AntiMPmod: Prediction of Antimicrobial Potential of a Chemically Modified Peptide From Its Tertiary Structure
metadata.description:
Welcome to the official repository for AntiMPmod, a computational method and web server for predicting the antimicrobial potential of chemically modified peptides from their tertiary structures. This resource is designed to support researchers in peptide therapeutics, antimicrobial drug discovery, and computational chemistry.

Web Server: http://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/antimpmod/ Structure Prediction Server (PEPstrMOD): http://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/pepstrmod/ Standalone (Docker): Pull image raghavagps/gpsraghava and run PERL code from the gpsr folder

Citation Agrawal, P., & Raghava, G. P. S. (2018). Prediction of Antimicrobial Potential of a Chemically Modified Peptide From Its Tertiary Structure. Frontiers in Microbiology, 9:2551. https://doi.org/10.3389/fmicb.2018.02551

About the Tool AntiMPmod is the first method developed specifically to predict the antimicrobial activity of chemically modified peptides using their 3D tertiary structures. Unlike all previous AMP prediction methods that rely solely on natural amino acid sequences, AntiMPmod leverages structural features extracted via SMILES format — including atom composition, diatom composition, molecular fingerprints, 2D chemical descriptors, and binary profiles — to handle the full diversity of chemical modifications.

The tool integrates data from:

SATPDB — Structurally Annotated Therapeutic Peptide Database (source of modified AMPs and non-AMPs) PEPstrMOD — for tertiary structure prediction of modified peptides up to 25 residues OpenBabel — for SMILES format conversion from PDB structures PaDEL — for computing molecular descriptors and fingerprints

metadata.description:
Background and Objective: Bacterial resistance to antibiotics is considered one of the most prominent and escalating global health challenges, which motivates the search for effective and safe therapeutic alternatives. Among these alternatives, antimicrobial peptides have emerged due to their unconventional mechanisms of action. Eumenitin peptide, extracted from the venom of a solitary wasp species, is regarded as a promising compound with multiple biological activities. This research aims to produce recombinant Eumenitin peptide using genetic engineering techniques and to evaluate its biological activity against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial strains.

Materials and Methods: The amino acid sequence of Eumenitin peptide was identified using the GenBank database, and gene-specific primers were designed via Geneious software to target the gene responsible for its expression. The gene was cloned and fused with green fluorescent protein (GFP) and expressed in Escherichia coli. The success of cloning and expression was confirmed through analysis of plasmid DNA sequencing. The efficiency of purification was assessed using fluorescence spectrophotometry and protein concentration assays. The antimicrobial activity of the produced peptide was evaluated using the Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion test against Gram-positive strains (Staphylococcus aureus, Listeria monocytogenes) and Gram-negative strains (Salmonella enterica, Yersinia enterocolitica).

Results: The results showed the successful production of recombinant Eumenitin peptide and its retention of biological activity, as clear inhibition zones were observed around the peptide-treated disks, indicating its antimicrobial activity against the tested strains.

Conclusions: This study confirms the possibility of producing Eumenitin peptide efficiently and at low cost through genetic engineering techniques, providing a promising alternative to peptides isolated naturally or chemically synthesized. The results indicate the potential development of Eumenitin as an antibacterial drug that contributes to addressing the phenomenon of antibiotic resistance.

metadata.title: Peptidos antimicrobianos de alacrán en la guerra contra bacterias multidrogo-resistentes
metadata.description:
RESUMEN

La resistencia antimicrobiana representa una de las principales amenazas a la salud. La Organización Mundial de la Salud (OMS) pronostica 10 millones de muertes al año, en 2050, ocasionadas por organismos resistentes a antimicrobianos. Los péptidos antimicrobianos representan una alternativa a los antibióticos convencionales, para combatir a las infecciones causadas por microorganismos a antibióticos. El veneno de alacrán es una fuente abundante de péptidos antimicrobianos. Estas moléculas se caracterizan por ser de naturaleza catiónica, anfipáticas y en estructura de α-hélice. Aquellos menores a 20 residuos de aminoácidos son ideales para su utilización debido al bajo costo que resulta la síntesis de moléculas pequeñas. El Uy234 es un péptido corto de alacrán que presenta actividad antimicrobiana contra bacterias Gram-positivas. Estudiar las propiedades que influyen en el mecanismo de acción de estos péptidos, es esencial para un diseño racional de terapias antimicrobianas.

 

ABSTRACT

Antimicrobial resistance represents one of the main health threats. The World Health Organization (WHO) predicts 10 million deaths per year by 2050 caused by antimicrobial-resistant organisms. Antimicrobial peptides provide an alternative to conventional antibiotics in combating infections caused by antibiotic-resistant microorganisms. Scorpion venom is an abundant source of antimicrobial peptides. These molecules are characterized by being cationic, amphipathic, and adopting an α-helical structure. Peptides with fewer than 20 amino acid residues are ideal for use due to the cost-effectiveness of synthesizing small molecules. Uy234 is a short scorpion peptide that exhibits antimicrobial activity against Gram-positive bacteria. Studying the properties influencing the mechanism of action of these peptides is essential for a rational design of antimicrobial therapies
